# Stars as suns, galaxies and the expanding universe (`stars_galaxies_cosmology`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/physics.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Physics, optics & astronomy (`physics`)
- Deps: needs heliocentrism; helped by astronomical_distances, spectroscopy, telescope, relativity
- Core idea: The stars are suns, so far away that their light takes years to thousands of years to arrive. The Milky Way is the disc of our own system of some hundred thousand million stars seen from inside; the faint spiral 'nebulae' are other such systems, millions of light years off. Their light is shifted towards the red in proportion to their distance: the universe is expanding and had a hot, dense beginning, now put at about 13.8 thousand million years ago. Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, which is why the Sun can last thousands of millions of years; elements heavier than helium were made in stars.
- Pitfalls:
  - Describing the Big Bang as an explosion into empty space from one point
  - Stating modern numbers as settled in an era where they were not (Hubble's 1929 scale made the universe younger than the Earth; the term 'Big Bang' dates from 1949, the decisive evidence from 1965)
  - Saying the Sun burns like a fire
  - Confusing the solar system, the galaxy and the universe
- History: greece: 5th c. BC – Democritus and Anaxagoras: the Milky Way is the light of many stars; Anaxagoras calls the Sun a glowing stone; islamic: 10th–11th c. – al-Sufi records the Andromeda nebula (964); Ibn al-Haytham and al-Biruni place the Milky Way among the stars; europe: 1584 Bruno: the stars are suns with worlds; 1610 Galileo resolves the Milky Way into stars; 1750–1785 Wright, Kant and Herschel on the Milky Way as a disc; 1927 Lemaître's expanding universe; americas: 1924 Hubble shows Andromeda is a separate galaxy; 1929 distance-redshift law; 1939 Bethe explains stellar fusion; 1965 Penzias and Wilson (Bell Labs) find the cosmic background radiation
- Read:
  - Edwin Hubble, The Realm of the Nebulae (1936)
  - Simon Singh, Big Bang (2004)
